R2: Prioritize how quickly incident response should be performed for each incident based on its scope, likely impact, time-critical nature, and resource availability.

R3: Select incident response strategies for active incidents by balancing the need to quickly recover from an incident with the need to observe the attacker or conduct a more thorough investigation.

N1: Every response strategy decision has trade-offs. For example, a strategy that supports observing the attacker’s behavior or conducting a more thorough investigation may be at odds with the need to quickly return to normal operations.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.MA-04: Incidents are escalated or elevated as needed
text:
RS.MA-04: Incidents are escalated or elevated as needed (Priority: High)

N1: Escalation generally refers to increasing resources or time frames, while elevation usually indicates involving a higher level of management in the response efforts.

R1: Track and validate the status of all ongoing incidents so that incidents in need of more response resources or a change in response strategy can be identified and the necessary changes initiated rapidly.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.MA-05: The criteria for initiating incident recovery are applied
text:
RS.MA-05: The criteria for initiating incident recovery are applied (Priority: High)

R1: Apply incident recovery criteria to known and assumed characteristics of the incident to determine when an incident’s recovery processes should be initiated.

R2: Take the possible operational disruption of incident recovery activities into account to determine when recovery should be initiated.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.AN: Investigations are conducted to ensure effective response and support forensics and recovery activities
text:
RS.AN (Incident Analysis): Investigations are conducted to ensure effective response and support forensics and recovery activities (Priority: High)

N1: The Incident Analysis Category focuses on investigating, determining, and documenting what has happened during an incident, as well as how and why it happened.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.AN-03: Analysis is performed to establish what has taken place during an incident and the root cause of the incident
text:
RS.AN-03: Analysis is performed to establish what has taken place during an incident and the root cause of the incident (Priority: High)

R1: Determine the sequence of events that have occurred during the incident and which assets and resources were involved in each of those events.

R2: Attempt to determine what vulnerabilities, threats, and threat actors were directly or indirectly involved in the incident.

R3: Analyze the incident to find the underlying or systemic root causes.

R4: Check any deployed cyber deception technology for additional information on attacker behavior.

N1: This information may also be helpful for identifying weaknesses in cybersecurity risk management that should be addressed to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.AN-06: Actions performed during an investigation are recorded, and the records’ integrity and provenance are preserved
text:
RS.AN-06: Actions performed during an investigation are recorded, and the records’ integrity and provenance are preserved (Priority: High)

N1: Facts discovered and actions taken during incident response tasks can be recorded by many means, including a paper logbook, audio/video recordings, or automatic session monitoring and logging, as permitted by the organization’s incident response plan and policy.

R1: Safeguard the confidentiality and integrity of incident response records, and ensure that only authorized personnel have access.

N2: Incident response records can contain sensitive information, such as data on exploited vulnerabilities, recent data breaches, and users who may have performed inappropriate actions. The incident lead is often responsible for ensuring that incident response records are properly safeguarded.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.AN-07: Incident data and metadata are collected, and their integrity and provenance are preserved
text:
RS.AN-07: Incident data and metadata are collected, and their integrity and provenance are preserved (Priority: High)

N1: Many incident responses involve the collection of incident data and metadata. Formal evidence gathering and handling using chain-of-custody procedures might not be performed for every incident that occurs (e.g., most malware incidents will not result in prosecution). However, collected incident data is still considered evidence, which is defined as “grounds for belief or disbelief; data on which to base proof or to establish truth or falsehood” [SP800-160v1].

R1: Collect and retain evidence from an incident in accordance with the organization’s evidence preservation procedures and data retention policies, and consider factors such as the possibility of prosecution, and the cost of retaining the data and the hardware and software needed to access the data in the future.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.AN-08: An incident’s magnitude is estimated and validated
text:
RS.AN-08: An incident’s magnitude is estimated and validated (Priority: High)

N1: Determining the incident’s magnitude is often one of the most challenging aspects of incident response.

R1: Look for indicators of compromise, evidence of persistence, and other signs of an incident on both the assets known to be targeted and other potential targets. Skipping this activity or performing it in a superficial way may cause underestimation of the incident’s magnitude, thus allowing the incident to continue indefinitely on other targets without the organization’s knowledge or monitoring.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.CO: Response activities are coordinated with internal and external stakeholders, as required by laws, regulations, or policies
text:
RS.CO (Incident Response Reporting and Communication): Response activities are coordinated with internal and external stakeholders, as required by laws, regulations, or policies (Priority: High)

N1: Incident response reporting and communication activities tend to fall into four categories. Incident coordination involves communicating current and planned incident response activities for a particular incident among the internal and external parties with incident response roles and responsibilities. Incident notification involves formally informing affected customers, employees, partners, regulators, or others about a data breach or other incident. Public communication involves communicating to the public about the status of a particular incident, such as responding to media inquiries. Incident information sharing involves sharing cybersecurity threat information with others, usually voluntarily, based on activity observed within the organization’s technology assets.

R1: Organizations should have mechanisms in place in advance to coordinate with affected parties about incidents when needed.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.CO-02: Internal and external stakeholders are notified of incidents
text:
RS.CO-02: Internal and external stakeholders are notified of incidents (Priority: High)

R1: When an incident is analyzed and prioritized, the incident response team should coordinate with the appropriate individuals inside and outside of the organization so that all who need to be involved will play their roles.

R2: Follow established procedures concerning incident coordination that include what must be reported to whom and at what times (e.g., initial notification, regular status updates).

R3: Perform notifications in compliance with the current incident notification-related laws and regulations that pertain to the organization’s sectors, geographic locations, customer locations, and any other characteristics that apply to the organization. Incident notification is an evolving topic, and new laws and regulations are being established frequently.

R4: Notify affected third parties of data breaches and other cybersecurity incidents in accordance with regulatory, legal, and contractual requirements.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.CO-02: Internal and external stakeholders are notified of incidents (part 2)
text: R5: Notify law enforcement agencies and regulatory bodies of incidents based on criteria in the incident response plan and management approval. Designated individuals should contact these parties in a manner consistent with the requirements of the law and the organization’s policies and procedures.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.CO-03: Information is shared with designated internal and external stakeholders
text:
RS.CO-03: Information is shared with designated internal and external stakeholders (Priority: High)

N1: Voluntary incident information sharing is often mutually beneficial because the same threats and attacks simultaneously affect multiple organizations. An example is sharing information about observed TTPs with a sector-specific Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC).

N2: Sharing defensive tactics between organizations can enhance overall situational awareness and increase the resiliency of all. There is a cost to threat actors to develop or purchase exploits and to deploy them. The effective identification and dissemination of detection techniques lowers the attackers’ return on investment and increases their costs.

N3: Incident handlers might coordinate their efforts with colleagues at partner organizations to share tactical, technical information on mitigating an attack that spans those organizations. The organizations participating in this type of relationship are usually peers without authority over each other. In addition to choosing to share information, they may also pool resources to solve common problems.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.CO-03: Information is shared with designated internal and external stakeholders (part 2)
text:
R1: Securely share information with stakeholders consistent with the organization’s response plans and information sharing agreements, including contracts with suppliers.

R2: Regularly update senior leadership on the status of major incidents.

R3: Notify human resources when malicious insider activity has occurred.

R4: Establish and follow media communications procedures for incident response that comply with the organization’s policies on media interaction and information disclosure.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.MI: Activities are performed to prevent expansion of an event and mitigate its effects
text:
RS.MI (Incident Mitigation): Activities are performed to prevent expansion of an event and mitigate its effects (Priority: High)

N1: Manually selecting containment and eradication actions may be easier and faster if the organization has criteria and procedures in place. Criteria could take the incident type into account (e.g., a cloud-based services compromise or a user endpoint ransomware infection) and use some of the risk evaluation factors in RS.MA. Another factor to consider is the duration of the containment measure (e.g., an emergency workaround that must be removed within hours, a temporary workaround to be removed within two weeks, or a permanent solution). The eradication measure’s duration could be similarly evaluated.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.MI: Activities are performed to prevent expansion of an event and mitigate its effects (part 2)
text: R1: In some instances, organizations redirect an attacker to a sandbox so that they can monitor the attacker’s activity, usually to gather additional evidence. This delays containment and eradication activities. The incident response team should first discuss the feasibility of this strategy with the legal department before executing it. The intentional delay can be dangerous because an attacker could escalate unauthorized access or compromise other systems.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.MI-01: Incidents are contained
text:
RS.MI-01: Incidents are contained (Priority: High)

N1: Containment refers to preventing the expansion of an incident. Containment can prevent additional damage and avoid overwhelming the organization’s resources. Most incidents require some form of containment.

C1: Consider configuring cybersecurity technologies (e.g., antivirus software) and the cybersecurity features of other technologies (e.g., operating systems, network infrastructure devices) to automatically perform some containment actions, like quarantining malware, transferring a compromised endpoint to an isolated remediation network, or halting the execution of an infected container.

C2: Consider authorizing third parties (e.g., the organization’s internet service providers and cloud service providers) to automatically act to contain certain types of incidents (e.g., large-scale DDoS attacks) on behalf of the organization.

R1: Allow incident handlers to manually select and perform containment actions instead of or in addition to automated containment measures.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RS.MI-02: Incidents are eradicated
text:
RS.MI-02: Incidents are eradicated (Priority: High)

N1: Eradication refers to mitigating an incident’s effects. After containment, eradication may be necessary to eliminate persistence mechanisms and entry points, such as deleting malware, disabling breached user accounts, and identifying and mitigating all exploited vulnerabilities.

R1: Identify all affected hosts and services within the organization so that all flaws and weaknesses can be remediated.

C1: Consider configuring cybersecurity technologies and the cybersecurity features of other technologies (e.g., operating systems, network infrastructure devices) to automatically perform some eradication actions.

C2: Consider authorizing third parties (e.g., the organization’s internet service providers and cloud service providers) to automatically act to eradicate certain types of incidents on behalf of the organization.

R2: Allow incident handlers to manually select and perform eradication actions instead of or in addition to automated eradication measures.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC: Assets and operations affected by a cybersecurity incident are restored
text:
RC (Recover): Assets and operations affected by a cybersecurity incident are restored (Priority: High)

N1: During incident recovery, personnel restore systems to normal operations, confirm that the systems are functioning normally, and (if applicable) remediate vulnerabilities to prevent similar incidents.

N2: Recovery operations include restoring systems from clean backups, rebuilding systems, replacing compromised files with clean versions, installing patches, changing passwords, and tightening security controls. In intrusions where the threat actor is highly sophisticated and the full scope of their tactics is not revealed, it may be necessary to go as far as replacing the hardware (e.g., bare metal) of all of the compromised systems.

N3: For more information on incident recovery, see [SP800-184].

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.RP: Restoration activities are performed to ensure operational availability of systems and services affected by cybersecurity incidents
text:
RC.RP (Incident Recovery Plan Execution): Restoration activities are performed to ensure operational availability of systems and services affected by cybersecurity incidents (Priority: High)

N1: Executing the incident recovery plan involves selecting, prioritizing, and performing recovery actions in a secure manner; verifying the integrity of recovered assets; declaring the end of incident recovery; and completing incident documentation.

N2: For more information on incident recovery plans and plan execution, see [SP800-184].

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.RP-01: The recovery portion of the incident response plan is executed once initiated from the incident response process
text:
RC.RP-01: The recovery portion of the incident response plan is executed once initiated from the incident response process (Priority: High)

R1: Begin recovery procedures during or after incident response processes.

R2: Inform all individuals with recovery responsibilities about the plans for recovery and the authorizations required to implement each aspect of the plans.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.RP-02: Recovery actions are selected, scoped, prioritized, and performed
text:
RC.RP-02: Recovery actions are selected, scoped, prioritized, and performed (Priority: High)

R1: Recovery actions should take timeliness, precision, and reliability (e.g., restoring only the affected files versus restoring all files) into account.

R2: Select recovery actions based on the criteria defined in the incident response plan and available resources.

R3: Change planned recovery actions based on a reassessment of organizational needs and resources.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.RP-03: The integrity of backups and other restoration assets is verified before using them for restoration
text:
RC.RP-03: The integrity of backups and other restoration assets is verified before using them for restoration (Priority: High)

R1: Check restoration assets for indicators of compromise, file corruption, and other integrity issues before use.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.RP-04: Critical mission functions and cybersecurity risk management are considered to establish post-incident operational norms
text:
RC.RP-04: Critical mission functions and cybersecurity risk management are considered to establish post-incident operational norms (Priority: High)

R1: Validate that essential services are restored in the appropriate order.

R2: Work with system owners to confirm the successful restoration of systems and the return to normal operations.

R3: Monitor the performance of restored systems to verify the adequacy of the restoration.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.RP-05: The integrity of restored assets is verified, systems and services are restored, and normal operating status is confirmed
text:
RC.RP-05: The integrity of restored assets is verified, systems and services are restored, and normal operating status is confirmed (Priority: High)

R1: Check restored assets for indicators of compromise, and remediate the root causes of the incident before production use.

R2: Verify the correctness and adequacy of the restoration actions taken before putting a restored system online.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.RP-06: The end of incident recovery is declared based on criteria, and incident-related documentation is completed
text:
RC.RP-06: The end of incident recovery is declared based on criteria, and incident-related documentation is completed (Priority: High)

R1: Prepare an after-action report that documents the incident itself, the response and recovery actions taken, and lessons learned.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.CO: Restoration activities are coordinated with internal and external parties
text:
RC.CO (Incident Recovery Communication): Restoration activities are coordinated with internal and external parties (Priority: High)

N1: Incident recovery communication is a continuation of the communication activities in RS.CO.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.CO-03: Recovery activities and progress in restoring operational capabilities are communicated to designated internal and external stakeholders
text:
RC.CO-03: Recovery activities and progress in restoring operational capabilities are communicated to designated internal and external stakeholders (Priority: High)

R1: Securely share recovery information, including restoration progress, consistent with response plans and information sharing agreements.

R2: Regularly update senior leadership on recovery status and restoration progress for major incidents.

R3: Follow the rules and protocols defined in contracts for incident information sharing between the organization and its suppliers.

R4: Coordinate crisis communication between the organization and its critical suppliers.

title: NIST SP 800-61r3 RC.CO-04: Public updates on incident recovery are shared using approved methods and messaging
text:
RC.CO-04: Public updates on incident recovery are shared using approved methods and messaging (Priority: High)

R1: Follow the organization’s breach notification procedures for recovering from a data breach incident.

R2: Explain the steps being taken to recover from the incident and to prevent a recurrence.

title: [INTERNAL] Authentication abuse (brute force, spraying, valid accounts): Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- repeated_auth_failures: at least 5 failures (default threshold) for the same service within the 60-second window.
- authentication_brute_force: a burst of failures for the same account and source (password_burst_same_account_source), or the same account from three or more sources (distributed_password_burst_same_account).
- A success after the failure burst from the same source raises the score (85 versus 75).
- Usernames carrying SQL indicators on flask_web are treated as SQL probing, not as account names.

title: [INTERNAL] Authentication abuse (brute force, spraying, valid accounts): Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Individual authentication events with service, source IP, username, status, count and timestamp source (log or application timestamps are preferred over receipt times).
- For a compromise claim: a success event for the same account and source after the failures, and activity of that session.

title: [INTERNAL] Authentication abuse (brute force, spraying, valid accounts): ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: T1110 Brute Force; T1110.001 Password Guessing; T1110.003 Password Spraying; T1110.004 Credential Stuffing; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1021.004 SSH

- T1110.001 when one account receives many passwords from one source; T1110.003 when many accounts each receive few passwords from one source; T1110.004 only when the tried pairs are shown to come from a credential dump; T1110 when the variant is unknown.
- T1078 only when a valid account is shown to be used; T1021.004 when SSH logins are used for lateral movement.

title: [INTERNAL] Authentication abuse (brute force, spraying, valid accounts): Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- A user or a scheduled task retrying with an expired or rotated password.
- Monitoring or configuration management with stale credentials.
- A NAT or proxy address aggregating many users.

title: [INTERNAL] Authentication abuse (brute force, spraying, valid accounts): Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Compare service, account, source and observation window across the events.
- Check whether any attempt succeeded and what the session did next (commands, new sockets, file changes).
- Review SSH keys and authorized_keys for unexpected additions after a success.

title: [INTERNAL] Authentication abuse (brute force, spraying, valid accounts): Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- For the lab Flask login: apply_rate_limit (HTTP 429 after three POST /login per ten seconds) or temporary_ip_block (HTTP 403) on a disposable peer for 300 seconds.
- For SSH or system accounts: lock or reset the account and review keys; firewall changes use the UFW transaction workflow.

title: [INTERNAL] Authentication abuse (brute force, spraying, valid accounts): Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Operator approval for any traffic intervention; lab traffic actions require a fresh direct-peer receipt.

title: [INTERNAL] Authentication abuse (brute force, spraying, valid accounts): Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Locking an account can deny service to its legitimate owner; blocking a shared address affects all users behind it.

title: [INTERNAL] Authentication abuse (brute force, spraying, valid accounts): Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Lab leases expire after 300 seconds or can be rolled back; account locks must be lifted manually after verification.

title: [INTERNAL] Beaconing and command-and-control triage: Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- http_beaconing: connections from one process to one destination with regular intervals; the rule treats coefficient of variation <= 0.25 with at least 4 intervals, or <= 0.35 with at least 8, as regular.
- DNS tunneling indicators: long high-entropy subdomains (entropy above 3.8 with 15 or more characters) or unusual query types such as TXT or NULL.
- Manager, loopback and Docker internal addresses are excluded from beaconing analysis.

title: [INTERNAL] Beaconing and command-and-control triage: Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Connection timestamps per process and destination; repeated observations of one socket count as a single connection.
- Process identity (PID, executable, start time) owning the sockets.
- Destination reputation and DNS evidence when available; DNS evidence is empty when telemetry only has the question.

title: [INTERNAL] Beaconing and command-and-control triage: ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: T1071 Application Layer Protocol; T1071.001 Web Protocols; T1572 Protocol Tunneling

- T1071.001 when the periodic traffic is HTTP or HTTPS; T1071 when the protocol is not identified; T1572 when the traffic is carried inside another protocol such as DNS.

title: [INTERNAL] Beaconing and command-and-control triage: Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Update checkers, telemetry clients, NTP, monitoring agents and keep-alive connections are periodic by design.
- Cloud CDN addresses shared by many services.

title: [INTERNAL] Beaconing and command-and-control triage: Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Identify the process and its parent, executable path and start time.
- Check whether the destination is expected for that software and whether the interval matches a known product.
- Look for related file writes, persistence entries or new processes around the first connection.

title: [INTERNAL] Beaconing and command-and-control triage: Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- If confirmed malicious: terminate the verified process tree, then isolate the host if other compromise indicators exist.
- If unconfirmed: increase monitoring and collect a network snapshot.

title: [INTERNAL] Beaconing and command-and-control triage: Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Verified process identity for termination; explicit confirmation for isolation.

title: [INTERNAL] Beaconing and command-and-control triage: Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Terminating a legitimate update agent or monitoring client causes loss of visibility or updates.

title: [INTERNAL] Beaconing and command-and-control triage: Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Process termination cannot be undone; restart legitimate software manually. Unisolate after cleanup.

title: [INTERNAL] Data exfiltration triage: Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Large or sustained outbound transfers from a host that normally receives traffic, especially after a compromise indicator.
- Outbound data over an existing C2 channel or over protocols not used by the service (DNS with high-entropy labels, unusual ports).

title: [INTERNAL] Data exfiltration triage: Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Flow records with bytes sent, destination and the owning process identity.
- Sensitive file access or file integrity events on the same host before the transfer.
- Without byte counts or file access evidence, exfiltration remains a hypothesis.

title: [INTERNAL] Data exfiltration triage: ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel; T1048 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol

- T1041 when the data leaves over the same connection or channel as the suspected C2; T1048 when it leaves over a different protocol than the C2.

title: [INTERNAL] Data exfiltration triage: Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Backups, log shipping, software uploads, container image pushes, file synchronization.

title: [INTERNAL] Data exfiltration triage: Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Identify the process, destination and time window; compare to normal outbound volume for the asset.
- Check which files the process opened or which sensitive paths changed.
- Correlate with earlier initial access or C2 evidence on the same Agent.

title: [INTERNAL] Data exfiltration triage: Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Contain the host (isolate keeps only the Manager channel) if exfiltration is ongoing and verified.
- Terminate the verified process; preserve evidence before cleanup.

title: [INTERNAL] Data exfiltration triage: Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Explicit operator confirmation for isolation and termination.

title: [INTERNAL] Data exfiltration triage: Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Isolation interrupts all services on the host; data already transferred cannot be recalled.

title: [INTERNAL] Data exfiltration triage: Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Unisolate after the transfer path is removed; termination has no rollback.

title: [INTERNAL] False-positive investigation: Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- An alert or incident whose only support is a score, a User-Agent string, a single repeated socket observation or an uncorrelated event.
- Desktop or remote-service activity (IDE helpers, browsers, update agents) flagged by process or network rules.

title: [INTERNAL] False-positive investigation: Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Process identity with PID, executable and process_start_time; a repeated observation of the same socket must not be counted as new connections.
- Distinguish a newly opened socket from a re-observed one (observation_count versus new_connection_count).
- Deployment thresholds, monitor mode, whitelist entries and the response policy in effect when the alert fired.

title: [INTERNAL] False-positive investigation: ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: none mapped

- Do not assign a technique when the evidence only shows a tool name or an anomaly score; mapping requires behavior evidence.

title: [INTERNAL] False-positive investigation: Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Administrative or maintenance work, scheduled jobs, configuration management, backups.
- Monitoring and health checks that are periodic by design.
- Authorized security testing.

title: [INTERNAL] False-positive investigation: Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- List each claim in the alert and the evidence ID that supports it; claims without evidence IDs are hypotheses.
- Check whether the process, user and destination are expected for this asset and time window.
- Compare with recent response outcomes for the same Agent (effective, ineffective, caused_side_effect, rolled_back_by_analyst).
- Record missing evidence explicitly instead of inferring it.

title: [INTERNAL] False-positive investigation: Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Mark the incident as false positive with a reason, add a narrowly scoped whitelist entry if justified, and keep monitoring.
- Do not dispatch containment or termination for an unverified alert.

title: [INTERNAL] False-positive investigation: Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- An analyst decision; incident resolution is separate from response actions.

title: [INTERNAL] False-positive investigation: Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Broad whitelist entries hide future true positives; scope them to executable path, user and destination.

title: [INTERNAL] False-positive investigation: Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Remove or narrow the whitelist entry and reopen the incident if new evidence appears.

title: [INTERNAL] Host containment (isolate / unisolate) and emergency recovery: Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Verified process or socket evidence on a Linux endpoint indicating active compromise: an interactive shell holding a network socket, confirmed malicious process tree, or confirmed command-and-control traffic.
- HTTP-only incidents do not qualify: host containment for an HTTP incident is refused and routed to AI Response Assist, because HTTP evidence does not identify a process.

title: [INTERNAL] Host containment (isolate / unisolate) and emergency recovery: Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Process identity (PID, process start time, executable path) or socket evidence tied to the same Agent.
- Confirmation that the endpoint is the affected asset and not only the observer of traffic.
- Asset role and business impact of losing network connectivity.

title: [INTERNAL] Host containment (isolate / unisolate) and emergency recovery: ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: none mapped

- Containment is a response, not a technique; map ATT&CK only from the incident evidence that justified it.

title: [INTERNAL] Host containment (isolate / unisolate) and emergency recovery: Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- The suspicious socket belongs to an administrator session or a legitimate service.
- The observed traffic was generated by a scanner against the endpoint rather than by the endpoint.

title: [INTERNAL] Host containment (isolate / unisolate) and emergency recovery: Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Confirm the Agent is online and authenticated before dispatching; containment is an ACK-confirmed command, not an optimistic state change.
- Check whether legacy containment (/tmp/isolated) is active: in that case scoped isolation refuses and requires local recovery.
- Record a snapshot; the response action service captures one before dispatch.

title: [INTERNAL] Host containment (isolate / unisolate) and emergency recovery: Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- isolate: the Agent creates the nftables table inet larp_containment with drop policies on input, output and forward at priority -150. It keeps loopback, IPv6 neighbor discovery, DNS (port 53) and the Manager channel: the resolved Manager addresses and the current WebSocket peer on the Manager port remain allowed, so the Agent can still receive commands.
- unisolate: deletes the larp_containment table. Use it after cleanup is verified.
- Isolation is stateful: it has anti-flapping cooldown (default 600 seconds) and an automatic rollback timer (default 300 seconds) unless configured otherwise.

title: [INTERNAL] Host containment (isolate / unisolate) and emergency recovery: Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Explicit operator confirmation (confirmed=true); system, policy_engine and risk_assessment actors cannot satisfy it.
- An enrolled Agent with nftables; existing UFW and Docker rules are preserved because containment uses its own table.
- No active cooldown for the same action on the Agent.

title: [INTERNAL] Host containment (isolate / unisolate) and emergency recovery: Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- All non-Manager traffic stops, including legitimate service traffic and SSH from administrators.
- If the Manager address changes (DNS) after isolation, the Agent may lose its channel.
- Automatic rollback may re-open the host before cleanup if the timer is left at its default.

title: [INTERNAL] Host containment (isolate / unisolate) and emergency recovery: Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Use unisolate from the Agents page; the action becomes applied only after the Agent ACK.
- Emergency recovery from the out-of-band console when SSH and the Manager channel fail: stop larp-agent.service and larp-firewall-apply.service, start larp-firewall-rollback.service, review journalctl for the apply, rollback and recover units, then check ss -H -ltnpe and ufw status verbose.
- If the state is rollback_failed: keep the Agent stopped, set LARP_UFW_CONTROL=0 in network.env, compare /var/lib/larp-agent/firewall-transaction.json with configuration and journal, restore only verified UFW files or the approved SSH path. Avoid resetting or flushing the whole firewall; keep Docker, containment and manual policies.

title: [INTERNAL] Network service scanning triage: Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- network_service_scanning: one remote source reached at least 8 distinct local TCP ports on the same endpoint within 60 seconds, observed as inbound sockets in ESTABLISHED or SYN-RECV state.
- HTTP requests from scanner User-Agents (automated_http_activity) against the same endpoint.

title: [INTERNAL] Network service scanning triage: Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Inbound socket evidence with direction, status, observation time and socket inode; duplicated observations of the same socket are counted once.
- The source and target addresses and the list of ports.

title: [INTERNAL] Network service scanning triage: ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: T1046 Network Service Discovery; T1595 Active Scanning; T1595.002 Vulnerability Scanning

- T1595 / T1595.002 for scanning from outside the organization; T1046 when the scan originates from an internal host as discovery.

title: [INTERNAL] Network service scanning triage: Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Authorized vulnerability scanning or asset inventory.
- Load balancer or monitoring health checks across several ports.
- Internet background scanning against an exposed host, which is common and usually not targeted.

title: [INTERNAL] Network service scanning triage: Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Check whether the source is internal or external, and whether it is a known scanner of the organization.
- Look for follow-up activity from the same source: authentication attempts, exploit requests, successful connections to services.
- If the scanning source is one of your own endpoints, investigate that endpoint for compromise.

title: [INTERNAL] Network service scanning triage: Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Monitor and correlate; scanning alone rarely justifies containment.
- For the lab Flask application, traffic intervention (block / rate limit) is limited to disposable documentation-range peers.

title: [INTERNAL] Network service scanning triage: Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Firewall changes on real endpoints go through the UFW transaction workflow with commit or rollback, not through incident response assist.

title: [INTERNAL] Network service scanning triage: Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Blocking scanners by IP is easily evaded and may block shared addresses.

title: [INTERNAL] Network service scanning triage: Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- UFW transactions not committed within 60 seconds roll back automatically.

title: [INTERNAL] Linux persistence checks: Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- File integrity changes to cron files, systemd unit files, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or web application directories.
- New processes started by cron or systemd that open network sockets or spawn shells.

title: [INTERNAL] Linux persistence checks: Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- The changed path and its SHA-256 transition from file integrity monitoring.
- The process or user that made the change when available, and the time of change.
- Maintenance windows or configuration management records that could explain the change.

title: [INTERNAL] Linux persistence checks: ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: T1053.003 Cron; T1543.002 Systemd Service; T1098.004 SSH Authorized Keys; T1505.003 Web Shell

- T1053.003 for a new or changed crontab entry; T1543.002 for a new or changed systemd unit file; T1098.004 for an added authorized_keys entry; T1505.003 for a new script file under the web application directory.

title: [INTERNAL] Linux persistence checks: Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Package installation or upgrade, configuration management runs, administrator changes during maintenance.

title: [INTERNAL] Linux persistence checks: Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Compare the path and SHA-256 transition against the expected configuration.
- Read the new cron entry, unit file or key comment; identify what it executes and which user owns it.
- Search for web shells: new script files in web roots and web server processes spawning shells.

title: [INTERNAL] Linux persistence checks: Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Quarantine the malicious file, remove the persistence entry, terminate verified processes started from it.
- Rotate credentials and keys that may have been exposed.

title: [INTERNAL] Linux persistence checks: Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Confirmation for quarantine and termination; a snapshot is captured before stateful actions.

title: [INTERNAL] Linux persistence checks: Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Removing a legitimate unit or key breaks services or administrator access; keep console access available.

title: [INTERNAL] Linux persistence checks: Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Quarantine is stateful and can be restored; restore removed configuration from the snapshot or backup after verification.

title: [INTERNAL] Reverse shell triage: Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- builtin_linux_network_shell: a shell process (bash, dash, sh, ash, ksh, zsh, fish) whose standard input/output file descriptors are bound to a network socket.
- A web service process (apache2, httpd, nginx, php-fpm, gunicorn, uwsgi, flask) in the ancestry of the shell.
- Interpreters such as python opening sockets and spawning shells; downloads with curl or wget before the shell.

title: [INTERNAL] Reverse shell triage: Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Process identity (PID, start time, executable), socket inode and file descriptors from the same sample.
- The socket holders: the rule does not assign a connection initiator; if several holders are equal, the primary process remains undetermined.
- Connection direction is recorded only when the TCP handshake was observed.

title: [INTERNAL] Reverse shell triage: ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: T1059.004 Unix Shell; T1059.006 Python; T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer

- T1059.004 when a shell holds the socket; T1059.006 when a python interpreter holds the socket; T1105 when a tool was downloaded before execution.

title: [INTERNAL] Reverse shell triage: Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Administrator SSH sessions, terminal multiplexers, remote development tools and IDE helpers hold sockets with interactive shells.
- Container exec sessions.

title: [INTERNAL] Reverse shell triage: Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Compare process identity, socket inode and FD on the same sample.
- Distinguish the socket holder from the process that created the connection.
- Check the parent chain for a web server or an unexpected interpreter, and the remote address for reputation.

title: [INTERNAL] Reverse shell triage: Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- kill_process_tree on the verified shell tree; isolate the host if the remote endpoint is confirmed malicious or the compromise path is unknown.
- Investigate the entry point (often T1190 against the web service) and persistence.

title: [INTERNAL] Reverse shell triage: Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- PID, start time, executable and parent PID; explicit operator confirmation.

title: [INTERNAL] Reverse shell triage: Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Killing an administrator session interrupts legitimate work; protected processes such as sshd are refused.

title: [INTERNAL] Reverse shell triage: Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Termination has no rollback; isolation can be reverted with unisolate after cleanup.

title: [INTERNAL] Session revocation for the lab Flask application: Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- The lab application granted a session (HTTP 302 on POST /login with a session_ref) for a request carrying SQL indicators, and the guard recorded a credential mismatch for that grant.

title: [INTERNAL] Session revocation for the lab Flask application: Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Classification sqli_exploitation_confirmed: a correlated grant_observation with credential_match=0, a matching flask_web AUTH_OBSERVATION success and the same request_id and session_ref within 5 seconds.
- A fresh direct-peer receipt for the same request.
- The session_ref (sha256 of the session audit nonce); Flask uses client-side signed sessions, so the cookie itself is not stored server-side.

title: [INTERNAL] Session revocation for the lab Flask application: ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1078 Valid Accounts

- T1190 for the exploitation that produced the grant; T1078 only if the evidence shows the granted session being used as a valid account.

title: [INTERNAL] Session revocation for the lab Flask application: Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- A legitimate login whose credentials happen to contain SQL metacharacters: in that case the credential check matches and no mismatch receipt exists.

title: [INTERNAL] Session revocation for the lab Flask application: Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Confirm the mismatch receipt and the session grant correlate to the same request_id.
- Review subsequent requests that presented the session to see what the session accessed.

title: [INTERNAL] Session revocation for the lab Flask application: Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- revoke_session: the Manager records the session_ref in the lab revoked_session table. When the signed cookie is next presented, the guard clears the session and returns HTTP 401; a revocation receipt with the action_id is recorded.
- Verification uses the revocation receipt for that action_id and session_ref.

title: [INTERNAL] Session revocation for the lab Flask application: Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Operator approval and execution; the investigation must still produce the same revoke proposal at execution time.
- The Flask session guard (session_denylist capability) configured for the Agent's lab adapter.

title: [INTERNAL] Session revocation for the lab Flask application: Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- The affected user must authenticate again.
- Revocation does not fix the injectable query or invalidate other sessions obtained the same way.

title: [INTERNAL] Session revocation for the lab Flask application: Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Irreversible for this cookie: the denylist entry is not removed. The user may authenticate again to obtain a new session.

title: [INTERNAL] SQL injection response with the lab Flask guard: Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- A stored web_access_logs row for POST /login on the flask_web service carries recognized SQL payload indicators (classification sqli_probe_observed).
- The HTTP client User-Agent matches a SQL testing tool such as sqlmap (classification sqli_tool_indicator) or a generic automated client (automated_http_activity).
- A request with SQL indicators correlates with an application session grant: HTTP 302 on POST /login with a session_ref and a matching AUTH_OBSERVATION success (sqli_exploitation_suspected).
- The lab grant_observation store records credential_match=0 for that request and session (sqli_exploitation_confirmed).

title: [INTERNAL] SQL injection response with the lab Flask guard: Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- The incident HTTP evidence group and its same-Agent web_access_logs rows; every row ID listed in source_event_ids must exist for the incident's Agent.
- For a confirmed exploitation claim: a correlated flask_web authentication success within 5 seconds on the same request_id and session_ref, plus an independently verified credential mismatch from the lab guard.
- A successful response code alone, or an authentication event that is not correlated by request_id, does not establish application compromise.
- For traffic intervention: a fresh direct-peer receipt in the lab observations store (not forwarded, at most 300 seconds old, within 5 seconds of the logged request).

title: [INTERNAL] SQL injection response with the lab Flask guard: ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application

- T1190 is mapped only for sqli_probe_observed, sqli_exploitation_suspected and sqli_exploitation_confirmed. Tool or automated-client indicators alone carry no technique mapping.

title: [INTERNAL] SQL injection response with the lab Flask guard: Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- An authorized penetration test or vulnerability scan against the lab application.
- A legitimate user whose password or username contains SQL metacharacters (quotes, comment markers).
- Automated health checks or crawlers that only resemble tools by User-Agent.
- Requests relayed through Cloudflare Tunnel or a proxy, where the logged source is not the real client.

title: [INTERNAL] SQL injection response with the lab Flask guard: Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Correlate request, authentication and endpoint observations for the same Agent, source IP and request_id.
- Run collect_additional_evidence: it gathers related Manager records two minutes either side of the observation (HTTP, authentication, flows, process metadata, incident notes) and requests a fresh authenticated Agent network snapshot. It is read-only and has no rollback.
- Check whether the session grant followed the injected request and whether the credential mismatch receipt exists.
- Review the web server for post-exploitation signs: child shells of the Flask process, new outbound connections.

title: [INTERNAL] SQL injection response with the lab Flask guard: Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- temporary_ip_block: the lab Flask guard rejects POST /login from the observed disposable peer with HTTP 403 for a 300-second lease.
- apply_rate_limit: the guard allows at most three POST /login requests per ten-second window from that peer; further requests receive HTTP 429 during the 300-second lease.
- revoke_session: offered only for sqli_exploitation_confirmed (see the session revocation runbook).
- increase_monitoring: review matching Manager HTTP records every 10 seconds for five minutes.
- generate_remediation_guidance: attach an evidence-linked note; fix the query with parameterized statements in the application.
- Verification: an action succeeds only when the lease is still owned and the guard recorded an HTTP 403 (block) or HTTP 429 (rate limit) receipt for that action_id and peer inside the lease window; otherwise it stays verifying, becomes expired after the deadline, or failed if the lease is gone.

title: [INTERNAL] SQL injection response with the lab Flask guard: Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- The proposal must be approved, then executed, by a scoped operator; the Manager re-runs the investigation and refuses if current evidence no longer supports the proposal.
- The peer must be listed by an administrator in the Agent's HTTP_RESPONSE_LAB_WAFS disposable_peers, must not be in protected_peers, and must be a host address in the documentation ranges 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 or 203.0.113.0/24.
- The lab adapter directory must be an absolute, existing path; otherwise the adapter is unavailable (HTTP 409).
- Only one active lease may own a peer; a second action is rejected while the first lease is live.

title: [INTERNAL] SQL injection response with the lab Flask guard: Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- The block affects every POST /login request from that peer, including any legitimate user behind the same address.
- Traffic intervention is unavailable for real (non-lab) peers: the captured HTTP source has no verified relationship to the enforcement point, and UFW firewall transactions are not used for this.
- A block does not remediate the vulnerable query; the attacker can return after the TTL or from another address.

title: [INTERNAL] SQL injection response with the lab Flask guard: Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Rollback deletes only the lease row owned by the action (peer and action_id) and verifies it is gone; a failure to verify returns HTTP 409 and the status rollback_failed.
- Rollback is available while the action is dispatched, verifying, succeeded, partial or rollback_failed.
- If no rollback is requested, the lease expires on its own after 300 seconds.

title: [INTERNAL] Verified process termination (PID plus start time): Observed indicators
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- A process with confirmed malicious behavior: an interpreter or shell spawned by a service, a process holding an unexpected outbound socket, or a process tree that respawns children.

title: [INTERNAL] Verified process termination (PID plus start time): Required evidence
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- The process identity tuple recorded by telemetry: PID, process_start_time, absolute executable path and parent PID. A bare PID or process name is not a target.
- The Agent ID that observed the process; PIDs are only meaningful per endpoint and per process start time because PIDs are reused.

title: [INTERNAL] Verified process termination (PID plus start time): ATT&CK mapping
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

Technique names from MITRE ATT&CK v20.1: T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

- Map the technique from the behavior evidence (for example T1059 for command interpreter execution); termination itself is not a technique.

title: [INTERNAL] Verified process termination (PID plus start time): Alternative explanations
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- PID reuse: the original process exited and a new process received the same PID; the start time and executable will differ.
- An administrator task or package manager that legitimately spawns shells.

title: [INTERNAL] Verified process termination (PID plus start time): Investigation steps
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Compare PID, start time, executable and parent PID with the current process list before requesting termination.
- Review the process tree to decide between kill_process (one process) and kill_process_tree (process and all descendants).
- Check the Agent self-protection result: protected targets are refused.

title: [INTERNAL] Verified process termination (PID plus start time): Response options
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- kill_process: terminate exactly the identified process.
- kill_process_tree: terminate the process and its descendants, children first, to prevent respawn.
- The Agent opens a pidfd for each target, re-checks (start time, executable, parent PID) before signalling, sends SIGTERM through the pidfd and waits up to 1.5 seconds for verified exit. If identity changes at any point the command is rejected.

title: [INTERNAL] Verified process termination (PID plus start time): Execution prerequisites
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Explicit operator confirmation (confirmed=true); automated actors cannot confirm.
- PID greater than 2, positive parent PID, finite positive start time and an absolute executable path.
- Protected processes are refused: init, systemd and systemd-* helpers, sshd, cloudflared, tailscaled, dbus, udevd, cron, containerd, dockerd, NetworkManager, kernel threads, and the Agent's own lineage.

title: [INTERNAL] Verified process termination (PID plus start time): Operational risks
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Killing a service process interrupts that service; data in memory is lost.
- If the parent respawns the process, a single kill only buys time; consider the tree or persistence checks.

title: [INTERNAL] Verified process termination (PID plus start time): Rollback guidance
text:
Internal LARP runbook (not an external authority).

- Process termination is one-shot: there is no automatic rollback and no cooldown. Restart the legitimate service manually if it was terminated in error.
